text.p: German trade unions, under heavy pressure to bow to free market concepts taking root elsewhere, lashed out on Wednesday against "unfettered capitalism" in Germany and across the globe.

The attack at the opening of a German Federation of Trade Unions (DGB) congress came as delegates prepared to discuss a controversial new "basic programme" of goals that would the first time commit German unions to market-based policies.
"I don't want an unfettered market economy and an authoritarian, anti-society republic," said Dieter Schulte, chairman of the DGB umbrella group representing some 10 million workers across Germany.

Karl Marx was right to warn of the "awful development of an unrestricted, unfettered world capitalism" in his Communist Manifesto of 1848, he told delegates at the congress in the east German town of Dresden.
Schulte side-stepped what could become a heated debate over the free market in the coming two days.

Instead, he used more familiar rhetoric in his keynote speech to charge Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government of having, in league with employers, "deregulated, privatised and scaled down (social costs)" over the last 14 years at the cost of rising unemployment and social injustice.

Schulte stressed that the DGB still saw full employment in Germany as an achievable goal and berated Kohl for his recent admission that a previous target of halving current jobless levels by the year 2000 could have been over-optimistic.

Recent protests over planned cuts to sick pay entitlements and the Bonn government's austerity package, aimed at securing German entry to the single European currency, demonstrated the strength of feeling against the current government, he added.
But the tough talk masked what some delegates believe could emerge in the federation's new basic programme as a commitment to policies that go some way towards those espoused by Kohl's government.
In a controversial phrase contained in the draft of the new programme, a "socially-oriented market economy" is described as "better-suited than other economic models to the goals of trade unions".

Such a statement would replace the hardline ideology that labour and capital are in basic conflict -- on which the existing 15-year-old programme is based but which has not prevented employers and unions from coming to regular deals in the past.
In his speech Schulte stressed the need for effective social and environmental measures to counteract the possible impact of the market economy on the individual.

Support for wide discussion of the programme came from metal and engineering trade union IG Metall, the largest union represented in the DGB, whose chief Klaus Wickel said in a statement the time was "ripe" for debate on the programme.

But with around 570 motions due to be heard proposing changes to the new programme -- and six calling for a complete postponement of the change -- Schulte acknowledged the possibility of vocal disagreement on the issue.
"Some of our opponents are hoping that we do ourselves some damage," he warned.
